patch.value: Flag lexicon conformance: one spelling per concept across every command, machine-checked, with a declared per-command flag budget

The consolidation programme shrinks the noun and verb surface. The flag surface is the other half of what an agent must learn and it is currently unconstrained: the same concept is spelled differently across commands, multi-value grammar is inconsistent enough to have its own defect item, stdin conventions differ per flag, and there is no ceiling on how many flags one command may accept — pm create alone publishes more than sixty. An agent's cost of using pm is the product of nouns, verbs, and flags, so consolidating only the first two leaves most of the learning cost in place. Establish a flag lexicon: every flag maps to exactly one declared concept, every concept has exactly one canonical spelling, value grammar is uniform per value kind (single, multi-value, path, stdin-capable, enum), and each command declares a flag budget that a new flag must fit inside or explicitly raise with a recorded rationale. The gate is mechanical, in the same conformance pass that checks the noun-verb table, so a non-conforming flag cannot merge. Every existing spelling survives as a hidden alias — this is a naming contract, not a removal.

A declared lexicon maps every flag on every command to exactly one concept with one canonical spelling and one declared value kind; The conformance gate rejects a new or renamed flag that introduces a second spelling for an existing concept, or a value grammar inconsistent with its value kind; Every current spelling remains accepted as a hidden alias, proven by a test over the full pre-change flag inventory; Each command declares a flag budget; exceeding it fails the gate unless the budget is raised in the same change with a recorded rationale; The lexicon is published as contract data so agents and completions consume it without prose; Measured flag-count and help-token deltas per command are recorded as evidence
One concept, one flag spelling, one value grammar, across the entire surface
Predictable flags remove the most common agent failure mode — a retry loop caused by guessing a spelling that exists on a neighbouring command
Adds a mechanical lexicon gate and hidden aliases for every current spelling; no feature is removed and no existing invocation breaks
An agent that learns pm's flag vocabulary once can predict the flags of a command it has never run

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
Flag-axis baseline measured 2026-07-25 (shipped 2026.7.25), for the per-command flag budget this item declares.

1,712 flag declarations across 77 top-level commands; 470 distinct spellings. Distribution is extremely skewed — the top five commands (plan 97, update 82, create 78, list 66, search 58) carry 381 declarations, 22% of the total on 6% of the commands.

Two candidate budget shapes the item should choose between, with evidence:
- A flat per-command ceiling would immediately fail on plan/update/create/list/search, which are the five commands agents use most; a ceiling low enough to be meaningful elsewhere would force real capability into subcommands or config on exactly the wrong surfaces.
- A tiered ceiling keyed to the declared surface tier (pm-kxci8x) fits the measured shape better: core-tier commands get a hard, small budget; specialist commands are allowed a larger one but must justify each flag against the shared lexicon.

Lexicon evidence for the "one spelling per concept" half: --author appears on 35 commands, --message on 30, --compact on 28, --force on 27, --limit on 25, --priority on 23, --parent on 23, --type on 21. High repetition is the healthy case — it means the concept is shared. The conformance risk is the long tail: 470 distinct spellings against roughly 77 commands means most spellings appear once or twice, and single-use spellings are where synonym drift hides. Recommend the gate measure the tail (spellings used on exactly one command) rather than the head.

value.text: Lexicon census 2026-07-29 giving this item a concrete acceptance target. The live surface is 84 commands and 1,792 flag occurrences drawn from 481 distinct spellings. Two hundred spellings, 41.6 percent, appear on exactly one command; 54 appear on ten or more; the shared head is --help 84, --author 33, --limit 30, --message 30, --force 27, --priority 26, --parent 24, --type 24, --sprint 23, --release 23, --assignee 22, --tag 20. Two hundred and two spellings cover 80 percent of occurrences, so the tail is long rather than negligible. Per-command flag budgets, which this item's title already promises, now have real outliers to bound: update-many 126, plan 97, update 84, create 78, and five list-family commands at 63 to 65 each. The strongest single finding for the budget rule is that create, update and update-many spend 288 occurrences, sixteen percent of the entire surface, re-declaring one item schema three times with divergent arity - that is the population a one-spelling-per-concept gate should collapse first, and it is measurable before and after. The second is that a singleton flag is indistinguishable from a shared one in the rendered surface, so the gate needs a declared local-or-shared disposition per flag rather than a similarity heuristic. Sequencing consequence recorded as ruling F on pm-pbyu: this item is upstream of the noun consolidation, not parallel to it.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
A concrete two-concept collision for the lexicon, confirmed from live help at build 2026.7.29.

The flag --file carries two incompatible meanings depending on the command:

On create and update, --file is item data. The value is a linked file path, in the form path=<value>,scope=<project|global>,note=<text>. The value is stored on the item.

On comments, notes and learnings, --file is an input channel. The value is a path the command reads the prose payload out of. The value is not stored anywhere; only the file's contents are.

Both meanings are load-bearing and both are the documented recommendation for their own family - the linked-file form because a bare colon-separated string stored through update --file is a known source of missing-path drift, and the read-from-file form because prose passed as a shell argument silently loses backtick-quoted content to command substitution. An agent that generalises one meaning to the other corrupts data in one direction and stores prose as a path in the other, and no error is raised in either case.

This is a clean test for the first criterion here: a lexicon that maps every flag to exactly one concept must split this spelling into two concepts with two canonical spellings, and the third criterion is satisfiable because the two meanings live on disjoint command sets, so both current spellings can survive as hidden aliases with no ambiguity.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text: Flag-budget evidence, measured 2026-08-01 at HEAD. pm create is cited in this item's description as publishing more than sixty flags; pm list publishes 69, which is the larger surface and the one an agent reaches first. Of those 69, 22 are presence predicates in three interchangeable spellings for the same concept -- --has-notes/--no-notes, --no-files/--filter-files-missing, --filter-ac-missing, --empty-body/--has-body -- so a single declared predicate grammar (pm-plwm's --where) would retire roughly a third of the command's flag surface without removing a capability. Also measured: the full per-command help surface is 218,872 bytes across 88 command spellings, about 54,718 tokens, against 9,701 bytes for pm contracts --summary. The flag surface is where that 54,718 lives.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text: Evidence measured 2026-08-07 for the one-concept-per-flag clause. Two live violations. First, --full denotes four different concepts: include heavy schema sections (contracts), the complete dependency row projection (deps), the complete graph row projection (graph), and expanded history entries (history). The value domain is boolean in every case, so the value-domain rule alone does not catch it — the lexicon needs the concept identity clause it already declares. Second, output bounding is spelled five ways across the surface: --output-limit and --output-budget as universal controls, and --limit, --node-limit, --edge-limit and --token-budget as per-command spellings, with deps carrying four of them privately. Recorded as evidence for the flag budget and the published lexicon.
